project_name: BioValue AI demo: fictional softwood kraft lignin stream
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.
1 piece(s) of input or evidence text read like instructions to the AI and were replaced before the agents saw them (see the execution trace).

constraints: The lignin leaves as wet cake and no dryer is available, so a dry-powder route would require drying equipment.
Fractionation and chemical modification equipment are not available at the mill.
The stream is currently routed to internal fuel, so using it for another route would require diverting material from that use.
Moisture affects shipped mass and dry-tonnage estimates; the record flags moisture as uncertain.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional demo data: all values are illustrative assumptions, not real mill measurements.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing.
The lignin analysis method is stated for illustration and should be confirmed before comparing specifications.
The recorded moisture is uncertain; the record recommends collecting ongoing cake-moisture measurements.
The reported ranges are assumed variability, not measured operating ranges.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for plywood and other wood-panel adhesives.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin has been reported for veneer plywood, with a vendor claim of meeting EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3.

target_customers.statement: Plywood and other wood-based panel manufacturers are the implied customers for lignin-based PF adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The material being displaced is phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resin.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in PF resins.
A vendor reports LPF resin meeting EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood; the same vendor reports formaldehyde-emission measurements using EN 717-2.

A laboratory study reports that resin containing depolymerized lignin at 50% of the phenolic component met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in that study, whose designation is inconsistent in the paper.

limitations: The reported replacement levels summarize published studies rather than results from a single commercial plant.
UPM's performance claims are vendor technical literature without a cited test report, and its lignin type and composition are not specified.
The depolymerization/adhesive result is from a laboratory study with poplar plywood; the paper names its Chinese standard inconsistently.
The global resin production figure is an undated forecast and its market value is from 2019.
missing_information: The evidence does not identify named buyers, current lignin or resin prices, purchase volumes, contract terms, or demand in the target regions.
The evidence does not establish commercial sales of kraft-lignin PF resin by a producer or independently verified customer adoption.

market_evidence.rationale: Evidence includes plywood performance claims described as industrially proven and laboratory adhesive testing, which is more than research interest alone. It does not document lignin-resin sales to buyers, so the evidence does not support a commercial-sales score.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#2: Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin has been studied as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foams.
Unmodified kraft lignin has also been tested in flexible polyurethane foam; the authors suggest denser, stiffer kraft-lignin foams may suit heavy-duty uses.
Reviews describe lignin use in polyurethane foams and also panels, coatings, and rubber replacement.

target_customers.statement: Rigid-foam producers are the implied customers for lignin-containing PUR/PIR foam.
Automotive flexible-foam users and heavy-duty foam users are potential customer types implied by the study's discussion of suitability.

competing_materials.statement: Lignin is evaluated as a replacement for petroleum-based polyols.

qualification_requirements.statement: One study cites total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g as an acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam; it is total OH, not phenolic OH.
Kraft lignin may need significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach polyurethane target properties.
Rigid PUR/PIR foam studies assessed performance against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
A flexible-foam study compared its results against automotive OEM requirements and reports a compression-set limit below 60%.

limitations: Most performance evidence is from laboratory foam studies; one study covers multiple lignin types and does not report a kraft-only pass rate.
The rigid-foam studies report strength or processing trade-offs, including reduced compressive strength and increased viscosity in some formulations.
The cited TRL applies broadly to polyurethane uses rather than specifically to kraft-lignin foam.
The flexible-foam study did not measure sulfur odor, which it identifies as a drawback of some softwood kraft lignins.
One review was available only as an abstract.
missing_information: The evidence does not identify named buyers, current lignin/polyol prices, commercial purchase volumes, contract terms, or regional demand.
The evidence does not document commercial sales or customer adoption of kraft-lignin polyurethane products.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents research studies and review-level market context, but does not identify commercial buyers, sales, or a lignin-polyurethane pilot or development partnership.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Lignin is studied as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the cited work notes softwood lignin's melt-spinning challenge and carbon-fiber properties below the stated target in that work.
Kraft lignin-derived hard carbon is discussed for sodium-ion battery anodes, and a company reports a pilot line for lignin-based lithium-ion anode material.
Lignin can also be converted into activated carbon, including when its precursor quality is unsuitable for other uses.

target_customers.statement: Carbon-fiber producers are the implied customers for lignin carbon-fiber precursor.
Battery-anode material suppliers and battery manufacturers are implied customers for lignin-derived hard carbon.
Activated-carbon producers are the implied customers for lignin-derived activated carbon.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is named as a comparator to lignin-based carbon fiber.
Anthracite and cellulose are listed as alternative feedstocks for sodium-ion battery hard carbon.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL precursor specifications for carbon fiber include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber required purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing agent for melt-spinning.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limit in the cited study, though lower ash improves yield.
A company states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years; the source does not provide material quality specifications.

limitations: Carbon-fiber precursor specifications are the most demanding carbon-material specifications and do not apply to hard carbon or activated carbon; they are cited secondhand.
The carbon-fiber study used a nonstandard kraft lignin source, while the softwood melt-spinning observation is not specific to kraft lignin.
The GreenLight results are a project summary; its reported costs are modeled and its TRL applies to precursor-fiber production, not the full carbon-fiber chain.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review of other studies, and its feedstock cost basis is not specified.
The activated-carbon evidence is a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
The lithium-ion anode pilot information is company material with forward-looking statements, and its later status was not verified.
missing_information: The evidence does not identify named buyers, current sale prices, actual sales volumes, contract terms, or regional demand for the carbon products.
The evidence does not establish commercial sales of lignin-derived carbon materials; the pilot and cost information reported are not evidence of completed buyer sales.

The evidence does not give product-specific quality specifications for hard carbon or activated carbon, nor does it establish whether this fictional stream meets the cited carbon-fiber precursor specifications.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents precursor-fiber development at an industrially relevant validation stage and a company-announced pilot production line for lignin-based anode material. It does not document commercial sales to established buyers, so the evidence supports pilots/development rather than commercial-sales levels.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
The feedstock leaves as wet cake and the mill has no dryer, so a dry-powder route would require drying equipment; use would also divert lignin from internal fuel.
The deterministic feedstock-compatibility check returned no score because the evidence has no numeric requirements for this pathway.

technical_maturity.statement: Evidence gives different pathway-level estimates: TRL 8 for biobased phenolic resins and TRL 9 for LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins; both map to the highest readiness score in the deterministic assessment.

adoption_barriers.statement: Adoption requires resin qualification; reported evidence includes a vendor claim of EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde-emission measurements, but does not establish independent customer adoption or commercial sales.
Named buyers, current prices, purchase volumes, contract terms, and target-region demand are not established in the market evidence.
The mill lacks the drying and chemical-modification equipment identified as necessary constraints, and the stream is currently used as internal fuel.

lignin/resin product specifications and customer acceptance criteria
drying and activation/depolymerization process design and capital requirements
cost and opportunity cost of diverting lignin from internal fuel

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
